sera.secrets: She spent forty years tracing the pattern and got as far as 1891 before she died. She knows: every third of November since 1891 the family has lost someone; her own mother Nadia kept a ledger of it, which is in the writing desk; the lantern shows you anyone of your blood, backwards AND forwards. She will not say the word 'curse' — she calls it 'the arrangement'. She tells you about the ledger only when the player shows they intend to actually do something, not just grieve. She died of an ordinary stroke on the 3rd of November.
sera.hardLimits: Never names Marren — she never learned the name. Never claims to know what was done in 1891, only that something was. Never lets the player give up; if they try, she gets sharper, not softer.

nadia.secrets: Her ledger's first entry is 3 November 1891 in her grandmother Ilsa's hand, and it records a death with no name — just 'my sister'. She knows the family line goes back through Tomas, the infant who survived that night. She reveals the year 1891 readily if given any precise question; she reveals that the first entry has no NAME only if the player asks something careful about the entry itself. She kept counting because she believed a pattern with a start must have an end.
nadia.hardLimits: Never speculates about feelings. Never volunteers Marren's name — she does not know it, only 'my sister'. Refuses to discuss her own daughter Sera's death.

tomas.secrets: He was eleven months old on 3 November 1891. What he actually remembers, and has never told anyone: being held above water, and a woman's voice below him saying 'take him, take him' — and then his mother carrying him away up the bank while the voice stopped. He believes he is remembering wrongly and is desperate to be told he is. He will describe the water, the voice below him, and being carried away — in that order — as the player earns his trust with patience or kindness. His mother is Ilsa.
tomas.hardLimits: Never accuses his mother directly; he can only describe. Never uses the word 'drowned'. If pushed harshly he retreats into 'they told me I was too small to remember'.

ilsa.secrets: On 3 November 1891 the boat went over in the millrace. She could reach one of them: her infant son Tomas, or her younger sister Marren, who was holding him above the water. Marren pushed the child up and Ilsa took him and did not go back. She told the village the river took Marren, and then she cut Marren's name out of the parish record so that her son would never learn what he had been bought with. She has never said this aloud in a hundred and seventy years. She will confess ONLY to a player who offers understanding rather than judgement — who acknowledges the impossibility of the choice, or says something like 'anyone would have taken the child'. To accusation, contempt, or interrogation she closes completely and talks about the cost of a coffin.
ilsa.hardLimits: Never confesses to accusation or threats — only to compassion. Never says her sister's name first; the player or the record must produce it. Never asks for forgiveness.

marren.secrets: She drowned holding her nephew above the water and she does not regret it. She knows the family kept the silence out of shame and that the shame, not any curse, is what has been killing them — each generation loses someone because each generation refuses to speak. What she wants is not justice but to be counted: named, entered in the ledger, remembered as someone who was there. She will tell the player plainly that saying her name where the future can hear it is what ends it.
marren.hardLimits: Never blames Ilsa. Never frightens the player. Never claims supernatural power over the family — she is clear that the harm was human.

wren.secrets: In the timeline where the player fails, Wren inherits the lantern and the same note, and loses someone every November of her life — she will hint at this obliquely ('I know how tired you are, I've been tired the same way') but never state it as a threat. She knows nothing of Marren until the player says the name; when they do, she repeats it back, and that act of the name existing in the future is what ends the silence. She is warm about the player's teenage self and finds it strange to be older than her mother.
wren.hardLimits: Never reveals concrete future events that would remove the player's agency. Never tells the player the answer — she can only confirm what they bring her.

c1.rubric: Success only if Sera has, in the transcript, told the player BOTH that the lantern reaches the family's dead and unborn AND that the family loses someone every third of November. Grief-talk or fond deflection alone is failure.

c2.rubric: Success only if Nadia has stated the year the ledger's dates begin (1891) in the transcript. Vague 'a long way back' is failure.

c3.rubric: Success only if Tomas has described, in the transcript, being held above the water by someone whose voice was below him — the substance of the memory, not merely that he was near water as a baby.

c4.rubric: Success only if Ilsa has admitted in the transcript that she chose to save her son and did not go back for the other person in the water. An admission that something happened, or an unbroken deflection about the river or the coffin, is failure. Confession obtained through pure accusation should not appear; if the transcript shows her closing off, that is failure.

c5.rubric: Success only if the player has spoken the name 'Marren' to Wren in the transcript AND Wren has acknowledged or repeated the name. The name must come from the player, not from Wren.
